lesson.title: After the Outage: Writing a Postmortem That Actually Prevents the Next One
lesson.summary: An incident postmortem is a structured, blameless review of what happened during an outage, built from packet captures and logs rather than memory, so an organization walks away with concrete fixes instead of just relief that the problem is over.
lesson.body:
Outages happen even in well run networks. What actually separates organizations that keep getting more reliable over time from ones that keep repeating the same failures is not luck, it is whether they systematically learn from every incident. Writing an incident postmortem is the standard industry practice for doing that learning on purpose, rather than hoping it happens informally after the fact, if it happens at all.

Blameless is not a nice sentiment tacked onto the process, it is a specific, deliberate practice with a concrete purpose. The goal of a postmortem is to understand what conditions allowed a failure to happen and to have a large impact, not to identify a person to hold responsible for it. This matters because if engineers believe they will be punished for an honest mistake, they will naturally become vague about exactly what they did, or avoid volunteering the specific command they ran or the specific assumption they made, and that exact information is usually what is needed to actually understand and fix the underlying problem. The more useful question is almost never why did a person do that, it is why did the system allow one person's plausible action to cause this much damage.

A useful postmortem has a fairly consistent structure. A timeline lays out what happened and when, built from evidence rather than from anyone's memory of a stressful event. An impact assessment states plainly who and what was affected, and for how long. A root cause section goes past the surface level description, not just that a router was misconfigured, but why that misconfiguration was possible in the first place, why it was not caught before it took effect, and why it took as long as it did to detect and reverse. Finally, a set of concrete action items, each with a specific owner, turns the analysis into actual change rather than a document that gets filed away and forgotten.

This is exactly where the technical material from earlier in the course becomes essential rather than academic. A packet capture from the time of the incident lets you see precisely what traffic was flowing, or not flowing, or arriving malformed, at the exact moment things broke, which is often the only way to settle a disagreement between two competing theories about what actually failed. Network logging, from device logs to routing protocol logs to firewall and application logs, provides the timestamped record needed to build an accurate timeline, since human memory of exact sequence and exact timing during a stressful incident turns out to be reliably unreliable.

Consider a routing change meant for a single data center that gets accidentally applied globally, and a portion of the network loses connectivity for several minutes. A packet capture taken from an affected host during the incident shows connection attempts going out with no response ever coming back, which confirms the failure sits at the network layer rather than in some application above it. Router logs show the exact timestamp the bad routing change was pushed live, and the exact timestamp someone reverted it, which anchors the timeline precisely and lets the team calculate exactly how long the impact lasted, rather than estimating it from memory. Notice what the resulting action items should look like: not be more careful next time, which is not specific enough to actually prevent a repeat, but something like requiring a staged rollout for routing changes so a mistake affects one location before it can affect all of them, and adding an automated check that flags any change whose scope is broader than what was requested.

A postmortem is only as good as what happens after it is written. Its real value is measured by whether the action items actually get completed and whether that same class of failure genuinely stops recurring, not by how thorough, well organized, or well written the document itself turns out to be.
